newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Continental sets sights on higher sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Continental sets sights on higher sales.

text.p: German tyre maker Continental AG on Tuesday reported higher sales and profits for the first three months of 1997 and said it expected a "significantly pleasing" profit for the year.
But the company warned it would step up restructuring efforts and may opt to close one of its three European commercial tyre plants if sales did not improve.

The group, which employs 46,400 people around the world, also said it would cut its workforce by at least 1,400 jobs, although some of these redundancies are linked to the introduction of a new manufacturing process expected to slash inventory and overhead costs.

Continental said first quarter pre-tax earnings rose to 88 million marks ($51.7 million) compared with 75 million marks in the 1996 first quarter following a 1.4 percent rise in global sales to 2.52 billion marks for the three-month period.

The Hanover-based group said at its annual news conference that it expected to post about five percent growth in sales to about 11 billion marks for 1997, but did not make a projection on potential growth in profit.
"We hope for a significantly pleasing increase in profits in 1997," Continental management board chairman Hubertus von Gruenberg said in a speech.
"As in 1996, the sources of earnings growth can be found in our many new high-tech products as well as internal productivity-enhancing and cost-curbing efforts," he said.
Continental shares were up 15 pfennigs at 38.50 marks in late morning trade but off the session high of 39.00 marks.

Von Gruenberg said that Continental in particular expected "clear earnings growth" in 1997 from its U.S.-based Continental General Tire unit, as well as at its ContiTech vehicle products division and from its European passenger tyre business.

The company in 1996 reported a rise in net income to 192.5 million marks, up 24 percent from 155.2 million marks in 1995. Sales last year rose 1.7 percent to 10.43 billion marks. The results included 160 million marks in restructuring charges.

Continental executives said a top priority for 1997 would be to invigorate lagging commercial vehicle tyre sales, which slumped eight percent in 1996 to 1.07 billion marks and forced the unit to report a pre-tax loss of 23 million marks.
"One of the most difficult challenges we face is to make a profit in the commercial vehicle tyre business," Von Gruenberg said. "This is a brutal market."

The drive to capture sales could force tough decisions. Continental currently operates plants in Germany, Belgium and Austria but has said the plants, which operate at 80 percent capacity and produce about 2.5 million tyres per year, were too small and have excessively high costs.

"If I had my choice, we would have two factories in Europe," said Stephan Kessel, who was named last week to take over the commerical vehicle business after the unit's former director, Klaus-Dieter Roeker, was forced to leave the group.

But Kessel said Continental would first target fleet managers in hopes of raising its sales volumes and seek to catch up with dominant French-based European market leader Michelin, which controls some 40 percent of the market compared with Continental's 15 percent market share.

Continental will also keep up restructuring efforts in its European passenger vehicle tyre unit, which posted a four percent gain in 1996 sales to 4.23 billion marks and a 34 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 335 million marks, despite 80 million marks in charges to close a factory in Ireland.
But Von Gruenberg did not rule out closing another European production plant, a long-time question facing the company.

Some savings may also come from Continental's patented "modular manufacturing process" which allow greater flexibility in producing smaller lots of specialised tyres and is expected to save the group about 50 million to 70 million marks year.
